title: WHAT IF THE “WORD FROM GOD” THAT BROKE YOU NEVER CAME FROM GOD?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE “WORD FROM GOD” THAT BROKE YOU NEVER CAME FROM GOD?

They said, “God told me to tell you.” You believed them. You cried. You changed your decisions. Maybe you even questioned your worth. But what happens when someone's personal opinion is dressed in God's authority—and you mistake their voice for His?
There is a particular kind of wound that doesn't come from an enemy.
It comes from someone holding a Bible.
Someone who prays beautifully. Someone who knows the right verses. Someone whose voice sounds so confident, so spiritual, so certain that questioning them almost feels like questioning God Himself.
And then they say six words that change everything.
“God told me to tell you…”
You stop breathing for a moment.
Because what comes next doesn't sound like advice anymore.
It sounds like heaven has issued a verdict.
Maybe they told you that your relationship was cursed.
That your suffering was punishment for a hidden sin.
That God was disappointed in you.
That you needed to leave your church, abandon a calling, marry a particular person, give a particular amount of money, or make a life-changing decision immediately.
Maybe they said your depression meant you lacked faith.
Maybe they looked at the most painful chapter of your life and confidently explained what God was supposedly doing, without ever asking what you had survived.
And because you loved Jesus, you listened.
Because you feared disobeying God, you obeyed.
Because you wanted to be faithful, you ignored the quiet questions rising inside you.
But later, when the room was empty and nobody could hear you, something inside began to ache.
Not because you hated correction.
Not because you refused to surrender.
But because the words that were supposed to bring you closer to God had somehow left you terrified of Him.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part was this:
You weren't sure whether you had been wounded by a person—or rejected by God.
Please stay with me.
Because what Scripture reveals about this is not only a warning to those who speak in God's name.
It is also a lifeline for those who have been crushed beneath words God never commanded anyone to speak.
And somewhere in this truth, you may finally discover that the voice which wounded you was never the voice of the Shepherd who died to save you.
In Jeremiah 23, God confronts a disturbing reality.
People were speaking as though they carried messages from heaven when their words were actually coming from their own hearts.
Listen carefully to Jeremiah 23:16:

“Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.” (KJV)
Read that last sentence again.
“A vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.”
In Hebrew, the expression is:
חֲזוֹן לִבָּם — ḥăzôn libbām
Literally, “a vision of their heart.”
The Hebrew word ḥāzôn refers to a vision or revelatory message. Libbām means “their heart,” referring to the inner person—the source of their thoughts, desires, and intentions.
In this passage, the contrast is devastating.
The prophets were presenting something as divine revelation when its actual source was themselves.
Not every powerful impression is a message from God.
Not every confident declaration carries heaven's authority.
Not every sentence beginning with “The Lord says” actually comes from the Lord.
And the frightening thing is that a person doesn't always need to be deliberately lying to become dangerously wrong.
Someone can be sincere and mistaken.
Emotionally moved and biblically confused.
Passionate about helping you and still overstep the boundaries of what God has revealed.
But sincerity does not transform human interpretation into divine authority.
And spiritual confidence is not the same thing as spiritual accuracy.
Jeremiah 23:21 records God's own words:
“I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran: I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied.” (KJV)
Imagine the weight of that statement.
They were running.
They were speaking.
They were active.
They appeared to be doing ministry.
But God said He had not sent them.
Their activity was not proof of divine authorization.
Their urgency was not proof of divine instruction.
Their religious vocabulary was not proof that heaven had spoken.
That should humble every preacher, teacher, prophet, pastor, ministry leader, and believer—including those of us who write about God's Word.
Because sometimes the most dangerous sentence a Christian can say is not an openly rebellious statement.
It is a personal conclusion introduced with the words:
“God told me.”
And before we point our fingers at someone else, we need to examine ourselves.
Have we ever used God's name to strengthen an argument we couldn't otherwise defend?
Have we ever mistaken our preferences for His commands?
Have we ever told someone what God wanted when, in reality, we were describing what we wanted?
Have we ever tried to control another person's decision by making our opinion sound like obedience to Jesus?
This is where the truth becomes uncomfortable.
Because spiritual manipulation does not always arrive wearing the face of a villain.
Sometimes it arrives through a well-meaning friend.
Sometimes through an admired leader.
Sometimes through a parent who loves you but cannot accept your choices.
Sometimes through someone who genuinely believes they are protecting you.
And sometimes it comes from our own mouths.
That is why this message is not an invitation to become suspicious of every Christian who offers counsel.
It is an invitation to become more faithful to Scripture than to personalities.
More committed to truth than to impressions.
More surrendered to Jesus than to the fear of disappointing people.
Because there is a difference between saying, “I believe this passage may speak to your situation; let's examine it together,” and saying, “God has commanded you to do what I am telling you.”
One invites biblical discernment.
The other may attempt to claim authority that belongs to God alone.
And that distinction can change someone's entire life.
Think about the person who was told, “God revealed that you must marry me.”
The person who was told, “If you leave this ministry, you are leaving God's will.”
The person who was pressured to give money because someone declared that their blessing depended on it.
The person who was instructed to remain silent about mistreatment because speaking up would supposedly dishonor God.
The person who was told that seeking professional help for emotional suffering meant they were not trusting Jesus.
These situations are not identical. They require different responses, and some involve serious abuse or coercion.
But they expose a shared danger:
God's name can be misused to make human demands appear unquestionable.
And when that happens, people may begin obeying the speaker out of fear rather than following Christ in faith.
Jesus never taught His disciples to surrender their consciences to every person claiming spiritual insight.
In Matthew 7:15, He warned:
“Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.” (KJV)
Notice the image.
Sheep's clothing.
Something familiar.
Something apparently harmless.
Something that resembles the community of faith.
But we must handle this warning responsibly.
Not everyone who gives bad advice is a false prophet.
Not every mistaken impression is deliberate deception.
Not every disagreement with a pastor is evidence of spiritual abuse.
Scripture calls us to discernment, not reckless accusations.
Nevertheless, Jesus' warning makes one truth unavoidable:
A spiritual appearance cannot substitute for spiritual truth.
And this is where the story takes an unexpected turn.
Because the Bible doesn't merely warn us about false messages.
It actually shows us what faithful believers should do when someone claims to speak God's truth.
In Acts 17:11, the Bereans are commended because:
“They received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.” (KJV)
They were listening to Paul.
The apostle Paul.
And they still examined the Scriptures.
Let that settle in your heart.
If examining Paul's teaching against Scripture was commendable, why would examining a modern preacher's claims be rebellion?
Why should asking for biblical support be treated as disrespect?
Why should a sincere question be considered a lack of faith?
The Bereans were neither gullible nor cynical.
They were receptive and discerning.
They listened with open hearts and examined with open Bibles.
That is not spiritual pride.
That is biblical maturity.
The New Testament gives an equally direct instruction in 1 Thessalonians 5:20–21:
“Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (KJV)
The Greek phrase behind “prove all things” is:
πάντα δὲ δοκιμάζετε — panta de dokimazete
The verb dokimazete means to test, examine, or evaluate for genuineness.
It is not a command to reject everything spiritual.
It is a command to test rather than accept uncritically.
And the immediate context matters: Paul is addressing the treatment of prophetic utterances within the Christian community.
He does not say, “Believe every claim because it sounds supernatural.”
Nor does he say, “Reject every claim because someone could be wrong.”
He says to test.
Then hold on to what is good.
Do you see the freedom in that?
You can respect someone without treating them as infallible.
You can receive correction without surrendering discernment.
You can appreciate spiritual counsel without allowing another person's impressions to become the final authority over your life.
And you can ask questions without abandoning your faith.
In fact, the more deeply you love Jesus, the more seriously you should care whether the words attributed to Him are actually consistent with His revealed truth.
Because His name is too holy to be used carelessly.
His people are too precious to be manipulated.
And His Word is too important to be replaced by someone's unchecked certainty.
But perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you have already been hurt.
Someone told you God had rejected you.
Someone declared that your past had disqualified you.
Someone took your failure and turned it into a permanent identity.
Someone spoke over your life as though your worst moment was the final chapter.
And you believed them.
For months.
Maybe years.
You kept hearing their voice whenever you prayed.
You opened your Bible, but instead of seeing the mercy of Christ, you remembered their condemnation.
You entered worship, but their words followed you into the sanctuary.
You tried to surrender to God, but you could not separate Him from the person who claimed to speak for Him.
If that is your story, hear this carefully:
A human being's declaration about you is not automatically God's verdict over you.
But don't simply accept that because I said it.
Open your Bible.
Look at Jesus.
Look at the way He confronts sin without surrendering truth.
Look at the way He welcomes repentant sinners without pretending their sins are harmless.
Look at the way He exposes religious hypocrisy while offering mercy to those who come to Him.
Consider the woman in Luke 7:36–50.
She enters a Pharisee's house, weeping at Jesus' feet.
Simon, the host, sees her through the reputation attached to her.
He knows she is a sinner.
And he silently questions whether Jesus understands what kind of woman is touching Him.
But Jesus sees what Simon has failed to see.
He does not deny her sin.
He does not pretend her past is irrelevant.
He speaks about forgiveness, love, and faith.
Then in Luke 7:48, Jesus says to her:
“Thy sins are forgiven.” (KJV)
And in verse 50:
“Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.” (KJV)
Imagine entering a room where people know your scandal.
Where your reputation arrives before you do.
Where someone has already decided what kind of person you are.
And then Jesus speaks.
Not to excuse sin.
Not to celebrate rebellion.
But to reveal the mercy available to a sinner who comes to Him in faith.
Simon saw her reputation.
Jesus saw the woman before Him.
And the Savior's words carried an authority Simon's private judgment did not possess.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that our feelings determine truth.
Not that repentance is optional.
Not that every painful correction must be rejected.
But that Jesus Christ—not human gossip, spiritual intimidation, or another person's private impressions—is the Savior and Lord before whom we ultimately stand.
And the same Jesus who forgave sinners also warned against falsehood.
The same Jesus who welcomed the broken also called people to repentance.
The same Jesus who exposed hypocrisy willingly went to the cross to redeem those who could never save themselves.
He is not a soft substitute for truth.
He is the truth.
And His grace does not leave us unchanged.
It brings us out of darkness.
That is why Romans 8:1 is so precious:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα — Ouden ara nyn katakrima
The word katakrima refers to condemnation, particularly an adverse judicial verdict.
Paul is not teaching that believers never need correction, repentance, or discipline.
He is proclaiming that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemning verdict of sin because of what God has accomplished through Jesus.
That is an astonishing difference.
Conviction exposes sin and calls us toward repentance and the mercy of Christ.
Condemnation, in the sense addressed by Romans 8:1, concerns the guilty verdict from which Christ delivers His people.
We must not confuse the two.
Sometimes a biblical warning will hurt because it exposes something we need to surrender.
Sometimes faithful correction will confront the very sin we have been trying to protect.
Proverbs 27:6 says:
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.” (KJV)
So no, the test of a message is not simply whether it makes you feel comfortable.
God's Word can pierce us.
Hebrews 4:12 describes it as sharper than any two-edged sword.
But faithful correction must still be truthful, grounded in Scripture, and consistent with God's character.
It should never require us to accept falsehood as obedience.
It should never make an unaccountable human voice equal to Scripture.
And it should never turn Christ's authority into a weapon for personal domination.
There is another passage we desperately need to remember.
In 1 John 4:1, the apostle writes:
John then emphasizes the confession of Jesus Christ come in the flesh.
His concern is not merely whether a message feels peaceful or sounds inspirational.
It is whether the teaching is faithful to the truth about Christ.
That gives us a crucial foundation.
A message must not be judged by emotion alone.
Not by tears.
Not by goosebumps.
Not by how loudly someone speaks.
Not by how many followers they have.
Not by whether they accurately guessed something about your past.
Not even by whether they can quote a Bible verse.
Scripture itself can be quoted out of context.
A true sentence can be used to support a false conclusion.
A biblical command can be applied to a situation God never intended it to govern.
That is why context matters.
Who was speaking?
To whom?
Under what covenantal circumstances?
What was the author actually communicating?
How does the passage fit within the whole counsel of Scripture?
And most importantly, how does our interpretation relate to the person and finished work of Jesus Christ?
We cannot build sound discipleship on isolated phrases and spiritual excitement.
We need the Word of God understood faithfully.
Consider the temptation of Jesus in Matthew 4.
Satan himself quoted Scripture.
He used Psalm 91 while tempting Jesus to throw Himself from the temple.
But Jesus refused to obey a distorted application of God's Word.
He answered with Scripture rightly applied.
Think about that.
A Bible verse in someone's mouth does not automatically make their conclusion biblical.
That sentence alone could spare someone years of confusion.
Because a person may quote “Touch not mine anointed” to silence legitimate accountability.
They may quote “Obey them that have the rule over you” while ignoring the biblical responsibilities and limits of spiritual leadership.
They may quote “Judge not” to prevent anyone from examining harmful conduct.
They may quote promises about blessing while neglecting repentance, suffering, perseverance, and the sovereignty of God.
And they may attach God's name to predictions Scripture has never authorized them to guarantee.
When biblical language is detached from biblical meaning, people can be led away from the very truth they think they are defending.
But here is something equally important.
We must not respond to spiritual manipulation by making ourselves the ultimate authority.
“I don't like that message” is not the same as “That message is unbiblical.”
“My feelings disagree” is not the same as “God's Word contradicts it.”
Discernment requires humility in both directions.
We must be willing to question others.
And willing to be corrected ourselves.
We must be cautious about claims of private revelation.
And equally cautious about our own assumptions.
We must refuse spiritual control.
And refuse the temptation to use discernment as an excuse for disobedience.
Because the goal is not independence from every spiritual authority.
The goal is faithful submission to Jesus Christ under the authority of His Word.
And this brings us to one of the most revealing questions you can ask when someone says, “God told me to tell you.”
What happens when you ask them to help you test it against Scripture?
Do they welcome careful examination?
Do they acknowledge the possibility that they may have misunderstood?
Do they distinguish between a biblical command and a personal impression?
Do they allow room for prayer, wise counsel, and responsible decision-making?
Or do they become angry?
Do they threaten you with divine punishment for asking questions?
Do they insist that questioning their words means questioning God?
Do they demand immediate obedience while discouraging accountability?
Those reactions do not, by themselves, prove whether a particular impression came from God.
But coercion, intimidation, and refusal of accountability are serious warning signs.
A faithful Christian leader should never need to pretend to be omniscient.
A mature believer can say, “I may be wrong.”
A trustworthy counselor can say, “Let's examine what Scripture actually teaches.”
And a person who truly fears God should be careful about claiming certainty where God has not given it.
James 3:1 warns that teachers will receive stricter judgment.
That should produce reverence, not arrogance.
Because speaking about God is a privilege.
Speaking for God without His authorization is a grave matter.
And there is a world of difference between declaring what Scripture clearly says and claiming that God privately dictated our personal opinion.
Perhaps this is the point where you need to stop thinking about the person who hurt you and begin asking what Jesus wants to heal in you.
Not every spiritual wound disappears when you identify the error.
You may understand that someone misused Scripture and still feel afraid to pray.
You may know their prediction was unreliable and still panic whenever you remember it.
You may recognize their manipulation and still struggle to trust a church community.
Healing can take time.
And if the experience involved abuse, threats, financial exploitation, or coercive control, seeking help from safe, qualified people and appropriate authorities can be a wise and necessary step.
Forgiveness does not require pretending the harm never happened.
Reconciliation does not eliminate the need for repentance, safety, and accountability.
And trusting Jesus does not mean placing yourself back under someone's control.
The Lord who calls His people to forgive also loves truth and justice.
He does not ask you to rename evil as good.
But He does invite you to bring your wounds to Him.
Listen to Jesus in Matthew 11:28:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (KJV)
Notice who is speaking.
Not the person who frightened you.
Not the leader who disappointed you.
Not the friend who claimed certainty about your future.
Jesus.
The One who knows the Father perfectly.
The One who never needs to exaggerate His authority.
The One whose words are true.
The One who carried our sins to the cross.
The One who rose from the dead.
And He says, “Come unto me.”
Not “Come to the person who claims to control access to Me.”
Not “Come after you have earned the approval of everyone who criticized you.”
Come to Me.
That invitation does not abolish the church, pastors, teachers, or the importance of Christian community.
Christ gives His people spiritual gifts and faithful leaders for their growth.
But every legitimate ministry exists to direct people toward Him, not to replace Him.
The shepherd is never the Savior.
The messenger is never the Messiah.
The counselor is never the Christ.
And your salvation is not secured by your ability to satisfy another person's spiritual expectations.
It rests in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again.
If you have been living under a declaration that made you feel permanently condemned, bring that declaration into the light of Scripture.
If it exposes a real sin, repent and run to the mercy of Christ.
If it contradicts God's Word, reject the falsehood.
If it is a personal prediction that Scripture does not establish, do not treat it as an unchangeable decree.
If it concerns a major life decision, seek wise, biblically grounded counsel without surrendering your responsibility before God.
And if you have been the person who used God's name to pressure someone, there is grace for you too.
But grace calls for honesty.
Perhaps you need to return to someone and say:
“I told you God said something when I should have admitted it was my own interpretation. I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
That apology may be one of the most Christlike things you ever do.
Because repentance is not humiliation for its own sake.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who forgives and transforms.
And this is why our theme matters so deeply.
The scandal may be that someone used spiritual authority to wound you.
The scandal may be that you once misrepresented God's voice yourself.
The scandal may be the hidden fear, bitterness, pride, or shame that grew from what happened.
But grace meets us in the truth.
Grace does not rewrite the Bible to accommodate our preferences.
Grace does not declare every human opinion holy.
Grace does not erase the need for repentance.
Grace brings sinners to Jesus Christ, where forgiveness is real and transformation becomes possible.
And perhaps the chapter Jesus is rewriting in your life begins with this realization:
You can stop treating every voice that mentions God as though it possesses God's authority.
You can open the Scriptures again.
You can learn to recognize faithful teaching.
You can ask careful questions.
You can receive wise correction.
You can confess your own sins without accepting accusations that are false.
You can forgive without abandoning healthy boundaries.
You can grow in Christ without living in fear of someone's next supposed revelation.
And you can rediscover the beauty of following Jesus—not because a human being has frightened you into compliance, but because His grace has brought you to repentance and faith.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear today.
Not another prediction.
Not another dramatic declaration about your destiny.
Not another person claiming to know every detail of God's hidden purposes.
Maybe you needed permission to return to what God has already revealed.
To read His Word carefully.
To trust His Son completely.
To seek His wisdom humbly.
And to remember that the Holy Spirit does not lead us into contradiction with the truth He has given through Scripture.
There is one more thing I want to ask you.
Not as someone claiming to know your private circumstances.
Not as someone pretending to have received a special revelation about your life.
But as a fellow human being pointing you toward the Word of God.
Whose voice have you allowed to become louder than Scripture?
Was it someone who told you that you would never change?
Someone who made you believe your past was stronger than Christ's mercy?
Someone who used fear to keep you from asking questions?
Or perhaps your own voice, repeating accusations that the Gospel calls you to bring before Jesus?
You do not have to answer publicly if doing so would expose you to harm.
But please do not avoid the question in your heart.
Take it before the Lord.
And remember this: your greatest need is not to discover a secret message about your future.
Your greatest need is to know the Savior who has already revealed Himself in the Gospel.
The cross tells us how seriously God takes sin.
The empty tomb tells us that death did not defeat His Son.
And the Scriptures call us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
And if you once used God's name carelessly, perhaps your response today is a quiet, sincere confession: “Jesus, forgive me. Teach me to speak Your truth faithfully.”
Your honesty may encourage another believer who thought they were alone.
Someone who still loves Jesus but has been wounded by religious manipulation.
Someone who needs to discover that biblical discernment is not rebellion against God.
We are not here to build a community that depends on one person's unquestionable opinions.
We want to encourage a community that opens the Bible, examines the truth, practices repentance, extends grace, and keeps Jesus Christ at the center.
And if these messages are helping you grow, I want to invite you to consider something deeper than simply reading the next article.
It can be an expression of Christian generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
But I want to be very clear about something, especially after everything we have discussed.
You do not need to pay us to prove your faith.
The Bible teaches generous, willing giving—not financial pressure disguised as divine command.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.

The heart of this work is to help people encounter the Gospel, understand Scripture more faithfully, grow in discipleship, and find encouragement to follow Christ through the ordinary and difficult moments of life.
You can still pray for this ministry.
You can still read and share the Gospel.
You can still encourage someone who is struggling.
Our desire is not to make people dependent on Gospel Warrior.
It is to point people beyond Gospel Warrior—to Jesus Christ.
Because if this article has taught us anything, it is that no human voice deserves the place that belongs to Him.
Not a preacher.
Not an influencer.
Not a ministry founder.
Not a writer.
Not even the voice behind these words.
Test what you hear.
Examine what you read.
Hold fast to what is good.
And follow the One who is worthy of your complete trust.
One day, the words that frightened you may no longer be the loudest words in your memory.
You may remember them, but they will not have to rule you.
You may still grieve what happened, but you will know where to bring your grief.
You may still have unanswered questions, but you will know where to seek truth.
And when someone says, “God told me to tell you,” you will not need to surrender your discernment in order to prove your devotion.
You can listen humbly.
You can test faithfully.
You can respond wisely.
And you can remember that the Savior who gave His life for you has not appointed every confident human opinion to rule your conscience.
The voice that broke your heart may have spoken God's name—but only Jesus Christ has the authority to define your standing before God.
